Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism

motor diagnosis · mimics · motor and nonmotor complicationsTypical Parkinson disease, a mimic, or a treatment complication?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Stage7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity establishes parkinsonism. Asymmetric onset and a clear levodopa response support Parkinson disease (PD); diagnosis is clinical
  • Early falls, vertical gaze palsy or early severe autonomic failure suggest another parkinsonian disorder. Dementia before or within 1 year of motor onset favors dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia)
  • Treat functional motor impairment with carbidopa-levodopa; distinguish wearing off from dyskinesia. Recognize nonmotor symptoms, including depression, even when movement improves
What it is

Progressive neurodegeneration; the commonest cause of parkinsonism

Driver

Loss of dopamine-producing substantia nigra neurons; alpha-synuclein aggregates form Lewy bodies

Triggers

Older age and inherited susceptibility (non-modifiable); male sex (non-modifiable)

Pesticides or solvents may raise risk; repeated severe head trauma is associated

Chain

Nigrostriatal dopamine falls thalamic inhibition increases motor-cortex activation falls

Insights

What can precede motor findings? A motor disorder can begin with nonmotor symptoms Nonmotor diseaseAlpha-synuclein pathology extends to olfactory, autonomic and brainstem structures; constipation, reduced smell and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder can precede motor findings

Why combine carbidopa with levodopa? Carbidopa limits peripheral conversion; levodopa reaches the brain Drug pairingLevodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and becomes dopamine. Carbidopa blocks peripheral dopa decarboxylase, reducing nausea and orthostasis while increasing brain delivery; central adverse effects such as agitation and visual hallucinations may still occur Treatment courseLoss of dopamine storage narrows the response window as disease progresses. Delaying levodopa has not been shown to prevent motor complications

What the disease does, by systemSupporting features, not diagnostic alone
MotorSmall handwriting, a quiet voice, reduced facial movement, reduced arm swing and short shuffling steps
AutonomicConstipation, orthostasis, urinary or sexual dysfunction
SleepInsomnia and dream enactment; REM sleep behavior disorder reflects loss of normal REM paralysis
CognitionExecutive and visuospatial impairment may precede memory loss
MoodDepression and anxiety may overlap motor slowing and masked facial expression
PathologyLoss of nigral pigment; Lewy bodies also involve cortex and autonomic structures
Parkinson-plusMultiple system atrophy involves glial alpha-synuclein; progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration are tauopathiesIn progressive supranuclear palsy, midbrain degeneration can give a hummingbird appearance on MRI
2Urgent risks
SwallowingDysphagia can lead to aspiration pneumonia

If swallowing symptoms develop, choose assess swallowing and aspiration risk.

New confusionAcute mental change requires assessment for infection and medication triggers

If confusion or hallucinations newly appear, choose look for a reversible trigger.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Parkinson diseaseAsymmetric slowing with rest tremor or rigidityProgressive; clear dopaminergic response; falls usually occur later
Toxic parkinsonismCarbon monoxide exposure or MPTP (an illicit-drug contaminant)Toxin exposure precedes motor disease
Essential tremorBilateral action tremor; head or voice may be involvedAction, rather than rest, brings out the tremor
Drug-induced parkinsonism Dopamine-blocking antipsychotic or antiemetic exposureAfter a drug start or increase; often symmetric; improves after withdrawal
Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia)Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations and dream enactmentDementia before or within 1 year of motor onset; marked antipsychotic sensitivity
Progressive supranuclear palsyVertical gaze limitation, gait freezing, early fallsEarly falls with vertical gaze palsy; usually poor levodopa response
Multiple system atrophySevere orthostasis or incontinence with ataxia or pyramidal signsEarly autonomic failure; poor dopaminergic response
Corticobasal degenerationAsymmetric motor signs with apraxia, cortical sensory loss or an alien limbCortical dysfunction accompanying parkinsonism; usually little levodopa benefit
Normal pressure hydrocephalusGait impairment, urinary incontinence and cognitive declineAsymmetric rest tremor and rigidity are less typical
Younger patient; liver disease with movement or psychiatric changesCopper-related disease, rather than typical aging-associated PD
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Early falls or vertical gaze palsyAtypical parkinsonismReassess for progressive supranuclear palsy
Psychosis during dopaminergic therapyDrug effect or advanced disease; also check triggersCheck infection and other drugs; reduce an implicated dopamine agonist first if feasible
Controlled motor symptoms with new anhedoniaDepression may need separate treatmentAssess and treat the mood syndrome

Pause point. A tremor alone does not establish PD. Demonstrate bradykinesia, review dopamine-blocking drugs, and look for early atypical features

5Diagnostic criteria
Parkinsonism Motor – Bradykinesia plus rigidity or resting tremor · PD – additionally requires no exclusion feature, supportive findings and few or no red flags
TRAPSS
  • Tremor – at rest
  • Rigidity – cogwheel resistance
  • Akinesia/bradykinesia – slow voluntary movement
  • Postural instability – usually late, not required for diagnosis
  • Shuffling gait – short steps
  • Small handwriting – micrographia
6Stage
Function and complications guide treatment
PatternAction
Mild disease with little functional interferenceIndividualize a lower-potency option or levodopa
Motor symptoms impair daily activitiesCarbidopa-levodopa provides the greatest motor benefit
Fluctuations or dyskinesia despite medicationAdjust therapy; consider advanced treatment when refractory
7Treatment
1

Firstmotor symptoms need treatment

Carbidopa-levodopa is preferred for most patients In practicePhysical or occupational therapy with exercise may improve conditioning Drug selectionFor selected younger patients with mild disease, pramipexole or ropinirole can be alternatives. Selegiline or rasagiline, monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitors, offer less potent symptom relief
2

Raiseend-of-dose slowing or recurrent off periods

Adjust levodopa dose timing; consider a dopamine agonist, MAO-B inhibitor or entacapone adjunct
3

Complicationtroublesome dyskinesia

Reduce or adjust levodopa for excess involuntary movement; amantadine can help AmantadineAmantadine can cause mottled skin (livedo reticularis), ataxia, peripheral edema and orthostatic symptoms
4

Rescuesudden off episode

Apomorphine provides rapid, short-acting dopaminergic rescue
5

Referrefractory tremor or persistent motor complications despite drug adjustment

Evaluate deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or internal globus pallidus
Medication complications
FindingAction or caution
Gambling, compulsive shopping or hypersexuality on a dopamine agonistReduce or discontinue the agonist; these drugs carry more psychosis risk than carbidopa-levodopa and may cause hallucinations or confusion
Older adult or cognitive impairmentAvoid dopamine agonists when possible; anticholinergics can worsen cognition, retention and constipation
Tremor predominates in a younger patientBenztropine or trihexyphenidyl may help tremor and rigidity, not bradykinesia; use cautiously because of anticholinergic effects
Levodopa adverse effectsDizziness, headache, agitation or visual hallucinations can occur early Timing and riskDyskinesia typically develops after 5 to 10 years of treatment; psychiatric adverse-effect risk rises with age, prior psychiatric illness, treatment duration and higher dose
Levodopa adjunct selectedEntacapone inhibits peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT); selegiline and rasagiline may amplify levodopa adverse effects Adjunct actionsTolcapone inhibits COMT both centrally and peripherally; the nonergot agonists ropinirole and pramipexole are preferred over ergot agents such as bromocriptine; ropinirole favors D2 receptors and pramipexole D3 receptors. Amantadine reduces N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor activity and alters dopamine release/reuptake
Nonmotor management
ProblemDo
Hallucinations or delusionsTreat triggers; reduce the implicated dopaminergic drug if feasible. Persistent symptoms may require quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin; strong dopamine blockade worsens movement
Depression or anxietyRecognize the mood syndrome even with effective motor therapy; for assessment and treatment, see
Dream enactmentMelatonin or clonazepam may reduce episodes
Orthostatic symptomsReview medications; consider salt intake or an abdominal binder when appropriate; persistent symptoms may need fludrocortisone or droxidopa
Parkinson disease dementiaConsider a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine Cognitive symptomsFor dementia with Lewy bodies, a cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil is a treatment option
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Every functional reviewReview dose timing, falls, swallowing, cognition, mood, sleep and orthostasis
Response becomes shorter or unpredictableSeparate off periods from excess involuntary movement before adjusting medication
Poor response or new atypical findingsReconsider the diagnosis and refer for neurologic reassessment
Practice
  1. A retired tailor notices shrinking handwriting and slower buttoning Examination shows slow repetitive finger taps, right-sided rigidity and a resting hand tremor Symptoms progressed gradually; eye movements are full and there have been no falls → Parkinson disease → Bradykinesia with asymmetric rigidity and rest tremor supports PD. Action tremor favors essential tremor; early falls and vertical gaze palsy suggest progressive supranuclear palsy
  2. An older adult develops gait freezing and repeated falls early in an illness There is axial rigidity and difficulty looking downward A trial of levodopa provides little improvement; hand tremor is not the dominant complaint → Progressive supranuclear palsy → Vertical gaze palsy and early postural instability with poor dopaminergic response favor progressive supranuclear palsy over idiopathic PD
  3. A patient with new parkinsonism reports severe lightheadedness on standing Urinary incontinence and a broad unsteady gait developed early Examination shows limb ataxia and brisk reflexes; levodopa has produced little motor benefit → Multiple system atrophy → Early marked autonomic dysfunction together with cerebellar or pyramidal abnormalities suggests multiple system atrophy
  4. An older patient develops cognitive fluctuations and formed visual hallucinations Within several months, rigidity and slowed movements appear The family also reports dream enactment; there was no preceding history of years of motor disease → Dementia with Lewy bodies → Dementia before or near the onset of parkinsonism, fluctuations and early visual hallucinations favor dementia with Lewy bodies; PD dementia follows established motor disease
  5. A patient with Parkinson disease takes carbidopa-levodopa on a regular schedule Walking slows predictably before each dose, then improves after the next tablet There are no involuntary writhing movements or hallucinations during the better periods → Adjust levodopa timing or add entacapone → Predictable end-of-dose slowing is wearing off. Adjust levodopa scheduling or add an adjunct such as entacapone; amantadine targets troublesome dyskinesia
  6. A patient develops compulsive online shopping after starting ropinirole The family reports new gambling losses despite previously cautious spending Motor function improved, but the behavior is causing financial harm; cognition otherwise remains at baseline → Reduce or discontinue ropinirole → New reward-seeking behavior is an impulse-control complication of a dopamine agonist; reducing or stopping the causative drug is the relevant intervention
  7. A patient has established Parkinson disease with increasing difficulty dressing and eating Bradykinesia and rigidity now interfere with daily activities There are no early atypical neurologic signs; the patient asks about the most effective motor medication → Carbidopa-levodopa → Levodopa gives the strongest symptomatic motor response and is preferred for most patients; an anticholinergic is mainly a selected tremor option and MAO-B inhibition is less potent
  8. A patient with Parkinson disease develops hallucinations after a dopamine agonist increase Attention is stable; evaluation finds no infection or additional culprit medication Symptoms distress the family, but the movement regimen has not yet been adjusted → Reduce the dopamine agonist if feasible → After checking reversible triggers, reduce an implicated dopamine agonist if feasible. If psychosis persists, select an agent with low motor risk rather than haloperidol
  9. A patient reports shaking while holding a cup or writing Both hands are affected and the voice sometimes trembles At rest the hands are quiet; repetitive movements are brisk, gait is normal, and rigidity is absent → Essential tremor → Symmetric action tremor with voice involvement and no bradykinesia favors essential tremor rather than parkinsonism
Pairs with Psychiatric Symptoms from Medical Illness or Medication: depression assessment and treatment despite controlled movement. Antipsychotic Adverse Effects: drug-induced parkinsonism and antipsychotic tolerability. Delirium: acute cognitive changes. Wilson Disease: a younger patient with hepatic and movement findings.
Transferable rule

Name the motor syndrome, check its chronology and drug exposures, then treat the complication actually present.
